questions.question: What are directives in Angular, and what's the difference between structural and attribute directives?
questions.title: Angular Directives: Structural vs Attribute
questions.direct_answer: A directive is a class that adds behavior to elements in the DOM. Angular has two main kinds: structural directives add or remove elements (changing the DOM layout) — *ngIf, *ngFor, *ngSwitch; attribute directives change the appearance or behavior of an existing element — ngClass, ngStyle, or a custom highlight directive. The asterisk (*) marks structural directives because they destroy and create elements (behind the scenes they become <ng-template>); attribute directives don't change the element count, they change what an element does or looks like.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can distinguish structural (add/remove elements, the *) from attribute (change existing elements) directives and give an example of each.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing the two: trying to use *ngIf to change styling, or ngClass to add/remove elements.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Structural directives add/remove elements (*ngIf, *ngFor); attribute directives change an existing element's look/behavior (ngClass, custom highlight). The * marks structural.

sections.title: Directives Add Behavior to Elements
sections.content: A directive is a class decorated with @Directive that adds behavior to DOM elements. Angular groups directives into two kinds. Structural directives change the DOM layout by adding or removing elements — *ngIf conditionally includes, *ngFor repeats, *ngSwitch chooses among options. Attribute directives change the appearance or behavior of an existing element without changing the element count — ngClass toggles classes, ngStyle sets styles, and a custom highlight directive can change an element's background. The asterisk (*) prefix marks a structural directive because it's syntactic sugar for an <ng-template>; attribute directives have no asterisk.

sections.title: Structural vs Attribute
sections.content:
Structural directives add/remove DOM nodes; attribute directives modify existing ones.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Structural ["*ngIf / *ngFor"]
    A[Element exists?] -->|no| B[Remove / not created]
    A -->|yes| C[Create element]
  end
  subgraph Attribute [ngClass / custom]
    D[Element exists] --> E[Change its style/behavior]
  end
```

sections.title: Structural and attribute directives in a template
Common Mistakes
items: Confusing the two: using *ngIf to change styling (it adds/removes elements) or ngClass to add/remove elements.
Forgetting the * on structural directives (ngIf without * is an error).
Writing a structural directive when an attribute directive (or just CSS) would do.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Directives add behavior to DOM elements; Angular has structural and attribute kinds.
Structural directives add/remove elements (*ngIf, *ngFor, *ngSwitch) — the * marks template sugar.
Attribute directives change an existing element's look/behavior (ngClass, ngStyle, custom highlight) — no *.
The * prefix means 'this is structural'; absence means attribute.
Don't confuse them: structural changes layout; attribute changes appearance.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: A directive in Angular is a class that adds behavior to DOM elements, and there are two main kinds. Structural directives change the DOM layout by adding or removing elements — ngIf conditionally includes an element, ngFor repeats, ngSwitch chooses among options. Attribute directives change the appearance or behavior of an existing element without changing the element count — ngClass toggles classes, ngStyle sets styles, or a custom highlight directive changes the background on hover. The asterisk prefix marks a structural directive because it's syntactic sugar for an ng-template; attribute directives have no asterisk. The common mistake is confusing the two — using ngIf to change styling when it actually adds or removes elements, or ngClass to add or remove elements when it only changes classes. The test is: does it change the element count? If yes, it's structural; if it only changes an existing element, it's attribute.
